items.title: Quasisymmetric homeomorphisms of the line and of the circle
items.statement: Let $|I|$ be Euclidean length for line intervals and round arc length for arcs of the circle, identified with $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$. An orientation-preserving line homeomorphism is $L$-quasisymmetric when images of adjacent equal-length intervals have length ratio at most $L$; equivalently, $\frac{h(x+t)-h(x)}{h(x)-h(x-t)}\le L$ for every $x\in\mathbb R,t>0$. An orientation-preserving circle homeomorphism is $L$-quasisymmetric when images of adjacent equal-length arcs have length ratio at most $L$. The line $1$-quasisymmetric maps are exactly positive-slope affine maps, and the circle $1$-quasisymmetric maps are rotations. On the circle this is equivalently expressed by a chordal metric control function $\eta$ on all triples, or by the uniform chord ratio bound on symmetric triples. Quasisymmetry is closed under composition and inverse; the inverse control is $\eta^{-1}_{h}(t)=1/\eta_h^{-1}(1/t)$, so its adjacent-arc constant is controlled by the forward constant and need not be the same. A disc automorphism normalized by $|\varphi(0)|\le r<1$ is $L(r)$-quasisymmetric, while the full automorphism group has no uniform quasisymmetry constant.
items.strategy: The line sup-form follows by taking the adjacent intervals $[x-t,x]$ and $[x,x+t]$. For the line $1$-case, swapping the intervals gives equality and the midpoint identity; continuity extends dyadic midpoint preservation to affinity. The circle $1$-case follows by partitioning into equal arcs and using continuity to recover all arc lengths. Arc and chord lengths on the unit circle satisfy $2s/\pi\le \chi\le s$ for $s\le\pi$; dyadic subdivisions give weak three-point control from adjacent-arc control, and Tukia--Vaisala Theorem 2.15 upgrades it to full metric control on the pseudoconvex, homogeneously totally bounded circle. The inverse and composition control functions are derived directly from the three-point inequality. For a disc automorphism with parameter $|a|\le r$, the boundary angular derivative lies between $(1-r)/(1+r)$ and $(1+r)/(1-r)$, giving $L(r)=((1+r)/(1-r))^2$. For $\varphi_a(z)=(z-a)/(1-az)$ with $a\uparrow1$, the image lengths of fixed adjacent arcs $[0,\delta]$ and $[\delta,2\delta]$ tend to $\pi$ and $0$, respectively.

items.title: A local Jacobian and energy bound for quasiconformal homeomorphisms
items.axiom_use: The Axiom of Choice is used by the geometric-to-analytic quasiconformality theorem and the differentiation-of-measures interface; Countable Choice is included for their completed-product ACL and measure conventions.
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Omega,\Omega'\subseteq\mathbb C$ be complex domains and let $f:\Omega\to\Omega'$ be an orientation-preserving $K$-geometrically quasiconformal homeomorphism, where $K\ge1$. Put $k=(K-1)/(K+1)$. Write $\partial_z f,\partial_{\bar z}f$ for its weak Wirtinger derivatives, $J_f=|\partial_z f|^2-|\partial_{\bar z}f|^2$ for its Jacobian, and $|Df|_{\rm HS}$ for the Hilbert--Schmidt norm of its real weak derivative matrix. Then for every relatively compact Borel set $E\subset\Omega$,
$$
\int_E J_f\,dA\le \lambda_2(f(E)),\qquad
\int_E |Df|_{\rm HS}^2\,dA\le \frac{2(1+k^2)}{1-k^2}\,\lambda_2(f(E)).
$$
items.strategy: Use the geometric-to-analytic equivalence and the locally finite pushforward-area measure. Differentiation identifies its absolutely continuous density with the Jacobian; the Beltrami inequality then bounds the real derivative energy by the Jacobian.

references.title: Mikhail Lyubich, Conformal Geometry and Dynamics of Quadratic Polynomials, vol. I
references.locator: Ch. 2 §11.4, Proposition 11.14, printed p. 181: the pushforward-area density and Jacobian-energy inequality (11.7)–(11.8); the sign typo in (11.8) is corrected from (11.6).

references.title: Christopher J. Bishop, Quasiconformal Mappings (Stony Brook Math 627 course notes)
references.locator: Ch. 3 §4, Theorem 4.2 and Corollary 4.3 (printed pp. 94–95), Lemma 4.4 and Corollary 4.5 (printed pp. 95–96): a.e. differentiability and the area-Jacobian/energy estimate. The differentiability proof has an unresolved step; see the Step 3b report.

items.title: Smooth arcs, lines and circles are removable for quasiconformal maps
items.axiom_use: The Axiom of Choice is used through the geometric/analytic quasiconformality interface at Steps 1.1, 2.1, 5.1 and 6.1. Countable Choice enters the completed-product Fubini and Lebesgue-measure interfaces at Steps 2.1–5.1; the cited fundamental theorem of calculus also states Dependent Choice, which follows from the stated AC. The curve-null cover and finite-intersection argument use no choice.
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K\subset\mathbb C$ be a compact subset of a straight line or a round circle, let $U\subseteq\mathbb C$ be open with $K\subset U$, and let $h:U\to\mathbb C$ be a homeomorphic embedding ([[def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps]]) that is $K_0$-quasiconformal on $U\setminus K$, where $K_0\ge1$. Then $h$ is $K_0$-quasiconformal on $U$, with the same maximal dilatation bound. For the sphere clause, a homeomorphism is $K_0$-quasiconformal when its local expressions in holomorphic charts are analytically $K_0$-quasiconformal ([[def-riemann-sphere-holomorphic-charts]], [[def-acl-sobolev-quasiconformal-homeomorphism]]). In particular, the same conclusion holds for a homeomorphism of the Riemann sphere that is quasiconformal off a round circle or a generalized straight line $L\cup\{\infty\}$.
items.strategy: On each component of U\K, use the geometric/analytic equivalence. Cover K by zero-area estimates and decompose R\K into dyadic squares; the local Jacobian/energy bound yields finite L2 energy up to K. Fubini and Cauchy–Schwarz give L1 coordinate derivatives on almost every line, and continuity plus the finite line/circle intersections glues the ACL restrictions. The ACL characterization then gives W1,2 on U; the Beltrami inequality holds a.e. because K is null, and the equivalence theorem returns geometric K0-quasiconformality. For the sphere clause, move a generalized circle to a compact finite circle in Möbius charts, apply the planar assertion, and use the chart composition interface.

references.title: Mikhail Lyubich, Conformal Geometry and Dynamics of Quadratic Polynomials, vol. I (book draft, Stony Brook)
references.locator: Ch. 2 §13.3, printed pp. 190-191: the Little Gluing Lemma (smooth version) and its ACL proof for piecewise smooth Jordan curves and arcs; read in full

items.title: The Ahlfors-Beurling extension formula for quasisymmetric maps of the line
items.axiom_use: Assume the Axiom of Choice for the analytic quasiconformality convention, invariance of domain, and the smooth-line gluing theorem. Countable Choice is used by the local finite-measure bound, the classical-to-weak derivative interface, and the gluing proof; AC implies Countable Choice by [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]. No choice is used in the formula, estimates, or properness argument.
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $h:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be an increasing $L$-quasisymmetric homeomorphism, $L\ge1$ ([[def-quasisymmetric-circle-homeomorphism]]), and let $\mathbb H=\{z\in\mathbb C:\operatorname{Im}z>0\}$ ([[def-unit-disc-upper-half-plane-and-blaschke-factor]], [[def-complex-domain]]). For $x+iy\in\mathbb H$, define

$$H(x+iy)=\frac{1}{2y}\int_{x-y}^{x+y}h(t)\,dt+\frac{i}{y}\left(\int_x^{x+y}h(t)\,dt-\int_{x-y}^{x}h(t)\,dt\right).$$

Then:

(a) $H$ is continuously differentiable on $\mathbb H$, maps $\mathbb H$ into $\mathbb H$, and extends continuously to $\overline{\mathbb H}$ with boundary values $H(x)=h(x)$.

(b) The real Jacobian determinant $J_H$ is positive everywhere on $\mathbb H$, so $H$ is a local diffeomorphism.

(c) With $C(L):=14L^3(1+L)$ and $k(L):=\sqrt{(C(L)-2)/(C(L)+2)}<1$, the Wirtinger derivatives satisfy $|H_{\bar z}|\le k(L)|H_z|$ on $\mathbb H$.

(d) $H$ is a homeomorphism $\mathbb H\to\mathbb H$. Pasting $H$ on $\overline{\mathbb H}$ to $H^*(z):=\overline{H(\bar z)}$ on the lower half-plane gives a $K(L)$-quasiconformal homeomorphism of $\widehat{\mathbb C}$ preserving $\mathbb R\cup\{\infty\}$, where $K(L)=(1+k(L))/(1-k(L))$.

(e) If $\widetilde h(x)=\lambda h(x/\lambda)+b$ for $\lambda>0$ and $b\in\mathbb R$, then its extension is $\widetilde H(z)=\lambda H(z/\lambda)+b$.
items.strategy: Define the two adjacent interval averages a and b, differentiate their moving endpoints directly, and write J_H=PS+QR. Adjacent equal-interval quasisymmetry bounds P,Q,R,S above and below, giving an explicit pointwise Wirtinger bound. Prove H tends to infinity at infinity using tail averages when y<=|x|/2 and chained adjacent-increment comparisons when y>=|x|/2; boundary convergence and this growth prove properness. Apply the proper-local-diffeomorphism and connected-cover theorems for H:H->H, then paste the analytic K(L)-quasiconformal maps on the two half-planes and apply the smooth-line removability supplier. Affine equivariance is a change of variables. The source's C-infinity regularity wording is weakened to C1; an odd square-root quasisymmetric witness shows the stronger claim is false.

references.title: Mikhail Lyubich, Conformal Geometry and Dynamics of Quadratic Polynomials, vol. I (book draft, Stony Brook)
references.locator: Ch. 2 §15.2.1, Theorem 15.4, printed p. 208: explicit formula and claims of positive Jacobian, bounded dilatation, properness and reflection extension; Exercise 15.5 asks for the omitted checks. The source's word 'smooth' is false for a general quasisymmetric h; this item corrects it to C1 and supplies an explicit counterexample.

items.title: The Beurling–Ahlfors extension theorem for circles and lines
items.axiom_use: Assume AC for the line extension, analytic quasiconformal composition, circular-dilatation, and smooth-circle gluing interfaces. Countable Choice is used through those measure interfaces and follows from AC by [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]].
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathbb D$ be the unit disc ([[def-unit-disc-upper-half-plane-and-blaschke-factor]]) and $\mathbb S^1=\partial\mathbb D$ ([[def-quasisymmetric-circle-homeomorphism]]).

(a) Every orientation-preserving $L$-quasisymmetric homeomorphism $h:\mathbb S^1\to\mathbb S^1$ extends to a $K(L)$-quasiconformal homeomorphism $H$ of the sphere such that $H(\mathbb S^1)=\mathbb S^1$, $H(\mathbb D)=\mathbb D$, $H(0)=0$, and $H|_{\mathbb S^1}=h$. In particular, $H|_{\overline{\mathbb D}}$ is a homeomorphism of the closed disc onto itself and is quasiconformal on $\mathbb D$.

(b) For every $0\le r<1$ there is $L(K,r)<\infty$ such that if an orientation-preserving $K$-quasiconformal sphere homeomorphism $H$ maps $\mathbb D$ onto itself and $|H(0)|\le r$, then $H|_{\mathbb S^1}$ is $L(K,r)$-quasisymmetric.

(c) Every orientation-preserving $L$-quasisymmetric homeomorphism $h:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ extends to a $K(L)$-quasiconformal sphere homeomorphism preserving $\mathbb R\cup\{\infty\}$ and fixing $\infty$. Conversely, if an orientation-preserving $K$-quasiconformal sphere homeomorphism $H$ preserves $\mathbb R\cup\{\infty\}$ and fixes $\infty$, then $H|_{\mathbb R}$ is $L(K)$-quasisymmetric.
items.strategy: lift a circle map to a periodic line map, apply the explicit line extension, and descend the periodic extension through the exponential covering. For restriction, normalize the image of an interior point and reflect across the circle.

references.title: Mikhail Lyubich, Conformal Geometry and Dynamics of Quadratic Polynomials, vol. I (book draft, Stony Brook)
references.locator: Ch. 2 §15.2.2, printed pp. 208–209, Lemma 15.6: normalized restriction from the disc and extension of circle quasisymmetries. Its proof invokes the global plane quasisymmetry estimate and sketches the symmetric extension; the periodic-lift descent below supplies those details for the extension clause.

references.title: Christopher J. Bishop, Quasiconformal Mappings (Stony Brook Math 627 course notes)
references.locator: Ch. 2 §8, printed pp. 78–80, Theorem 8.1: both directions of the line extension theorem; the restriction direction is proved by the modulus of a normalized annulus, and the extension direction by a hyperbolic pentagon tessellation.

items.title: Quasicircles, quasidisks and quasiarcs
items.axiom_use: The Axiom of Choice is assumed through the analytic quasiconformal interface and the Jordan–Brouwer separation theorem. The referenced geometric convention carries Countable Choice for modulus; AC implies it. The definitions themselves make no selections.
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Write $\widehat{\mathbb C}=\mathbb C\cup\{\infty\}$ for the Riemann sphere with its standard holomorphic charts ([[rem-riemann-sphere-one-point-compactification]], [[def-riemann-sphere-holomorphic-charts]]). Put $\mathbb T=\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|=1\}$ and $\mathbb D=\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|<1\}$. Identify the quotient circle $\mathbb S^1=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with $\mathbb T$ by $[t]\mapsto e^{2\pi i t}$ ([[def-circle-as-real-line-mod-integers]], [[thm-real-line-mod-integers-is-homeomorphic-to-the-unit-circle]]). A **Jordan curve** in $\widehat{\mathbb C}$ is the image of a topological embedding $\mathbb S^1\hookrightarrow\widehat{\mathbb C}$ ([[def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps]]); by [[thm-jordan-brouwer-separation]] it has exactly two complementary components with common boundary. A sphere homeomorphism is **$K$-quasiconformal** if it preserves the standard complex orientation ([[def-geometric-quasiconformal-homeomorphism]]) and, in every connected holomorphic chart neighborhood, its coordinate expression is $K$-quasiconformal in the analytic sense ([[def-acl-sobolev-quasiconformal-homeomorphism]]); $K\ge1$ is a uniform upper bound for the local dilatations.

(a) A Jordan curve $\Gamma\subseteq\widehat{\mathbb C}$ is a **$K$-quasicircle** if $\Gamma=F(\mathbb T)$ for a $K$-quasiconformal sphere homeomorphism $F$. It is a **quasicircle** if it is a $K$-quasicircle for some finite $K$. Its **quasicircle constant** is
$$K(\Gamma)=\inf\{K\ge1:\Gamma=F(\mathbb T)\text{ for some }K\text{-quasiconformal sphere homeomorphism }F\}.$$
The infimum is not asserted to be attained.

(b) A domain $U\subseteq\widehat{\mathbb C}$ is a **$K$-quasidisk** if $U=G(\mathbb D)$ for a $K$-quasiconformal sphere homeomorphism $G$; it is a quasidisk if this holds for some finite $K$. The two complementary components of a $K$-quasicircle are $K$-quasidisks.

(c) A **$K$-quasiarc** is the image of the open line segment $(-1,1)\subset\mathbb C$ under a $K$-quasiconformal homeomorphism of $\mathbb C$; a **quasiarc** is a $K$-quasiarc for some finite $K$. A **$K$-quasiline** is the image of $\mathbb R$ under a $K$-quasiconformal homeomorphism of $\mathbb C$; a **quasiline** is a $K$-quasiline for some finite $K$.

(d) Quasicircles are Möbius invariant with unchanged constant: for every Möbius transformation $M$,
$$K(M(\Gamma))=K(\Gamma).$$
items.strategy: For a K-quasicircle F(T), the round circle parametrization makes it a Jordan curve. A sphere homeomorphism carries the standard complementary components D and (z↦1/z)(D) to its two complementary components; both are K-quasidisks, using quasiconformal composition for the second. For Möbius invariance, postcompose a representing map with M and then with M^{-1} for the converse; this makes the admissible sets of constants identical. Quasiarcs use a line segment, while quasilines use R.

references.title: Frederick W. Gehring, Characterizations of quasidisks, Banach Center Publications 48 (1999)
references.locator: §I.A–B, printed pp. 12–15: quasiconformal definitions and quasidisks as images of a disk or half-plane under a quasiconformal sphere self-map; read in full

references.title: Gaven J. Martin, Stream lines, quasilines and holomorphic motions, Complex Analysis and its Synergies 1 (2015), article 5
references.locator: §1, paragraph beginning “A quasi-arc, respectively quasiline, quasicircle”: quasiarcs as quasiconformal images of a line segment, quasilines of the real line, quasicircles of the round circle; K-prefix convention; read in full

items.title: Riemann maps of Jordan domains extend to homeomorphisms of the closures
items.axiom_use: Full AC is used by the Riemann mapping theorem, Jordan–Schönflies, and Jordan–Brouwer separation. AC implies Countable Choice, which the extremal-length, modulus, and Lebesgue-area interfaces assume; Countable Choice also selects one short crosscut at each dyadic scale.
items.statement: Assume AC. Every complementary component of a Jordan curve on the sphere is conformally equivalent to the unit disk, and every conformal equivalence extends uniquely to a homeomorphism of closures. After a Möbius normalization placing the curve in C, the exterior map can be normalized to fix infinity. If the original curve contains infinity, this last normalization is asserted only after changing coordinates, since no exterior map fixing infinity exists when infinity is on the boundary.
items.strategy: Use Jordan–Brouwer and Jordan–Schönflies to get two Jordan domains with disk closures. Verify the homological simple-connectivity hypothesis of the Riemann mapping theorem from connected complements and the locally constant index theorem, obtaining the interior map and, after inversion about a point of the bounded component, the normalized exterior map. For an arbitrary Riemann map, transport a boundary prime end to a half-plane chart. The half-annulus semicircle family has extremal length π/log 2 by the logarithm-to-rectangle map; its conformal images in the bounded domain lie in disjoint half-annulus images of total finite area, so countable choice gives a nest of cross-cuts with lengths tending to zero. Lyubich’s Carathéodory–Torhorst prime-end argument then gives continuous extension because the complementary Jordan closure is locally connected; Jordan–Schönflies identifies prime ends one-to-one with physical boundary points, making the extension a homeomorphism. The scaffold’s unconditional exterior-infinity normalization is false for a Jordan curve through infinity, so the statement now qualifies that normalization after a Möbius change of coordinates.

references.title: Mikhail Lyubich, Conformal Geometry and Dynamics of Quadratic Polynomials, vol. I (book draft, Stony Brook)
references.locator: Ch. 1 §§8.1–8.2, printed pp. 146–150: Lemma 8.4 (shrinking cross-cuts by extremal length), the Carathéodory–Torhorst argument, and the Conformal Schönflies Theorem; read in full.

references.title: Christopher J. Bishop, Quasiconformal Mappings (Stony Brook Math 627 course notes)
references.locator: Ch. 1 §4, printed pp. 29–35, including Theorem 4.7 at p. 32 and its proof of continuous boundary extension for locally path-connected boundaries; §5, printed p. 37, the Jordan-domain homeomorphic boundary statement; read in full.

items.title: Bounded turning, quasiconformal images of the circle, and quasiconformal reflections
items.axiom_use: Assume AC for the ACL quasiconformal convention, the Jordan-boundary maps, Beurling–Ahlfors extension, composition and smooth-curve gluing. Countable Choice is used by the extremal-length and gluing interfaces and follows from AC by [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]].
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\Gamma\subset\widehat{\mathbb C}$ be a Jordan curve. For clause (ii), choose a Möbius coordinate $\chi$ with $\infty\notin\chi(\Gamma)$ and measure Euclidean distances and diameters on $\chi(\Gamma)$. The equivalent four-point formulation below is Möbius invariant, so the criterion applies to curves in any sphere position.

(i) $\Gamma$ is a $K$-quasicircle: it is the image of $\mathbb S^1$ under a $K$-quasiconformal sphere homeomorphism ([[def-quasicircle]]).

(ii) $\Gamma$ has **bounded turning** with constant $M$: for every $x,y\in\chi(\Gamma)$, one of the two arcs $\delta\subset\chi(\Gamma)$ with endpoints $x,y$ satisfies $\operatorname{diam}\delta\le M|x-y|$. Equivalently, if $\gamma_1,\gamma_2$ are the components of $\chi(\Gamma)\setminus\{x,y\}$, then $\min_j\operatorname{diam}\gamma_j\le M|x-y|$. Equivalently, for every four distinct points in alternating order, so that $z_1,z_3$ separate $z_2,z_4$ on the curve,
$$|z_1-z_2||z_3-z_4|+|z_2-z_3||z_4-z_1|\le b|z_1-z_3||z_2-z_4|.$$
The constants satisfy the explicit implications $b=2M(M+1)$ and $M=2b$.

(iii) $\Gamma$ admits a **quasiconformal reflection**: an orientation-reversing quasiconformal involution $\sigma:\widehat{\mathbb C}\to\widehat{\mathbb C}$ with $\sigma^2=\mathrm{id}$, fixed-point set exactly $\Gamma$, and which interchanges the two complementary components.

The three conditions are equivalent with quantitative control: each of $K$, $M$, and the reflection dilatation can be bounded by a function of either of the others. No closed formula for these general functions is asserted.
items.strategy: use the cross-ratio form of bounded turning, Ahlfors's extremal-distance criterion for reflection, the line Beurling–Ahlfors extension, and gluing across a smooth source circle.

references.title: Lars V. Ahlfors, Quasiconformal reflections, Acta Mathematica 109 (1963), 291–301
references.locator: Part I §§2–5, printed English Acta pp. 294–297 (Mathnet translation pp. 105–108): Lemmas 1–2 and Theorem 1 characterize curves admitting a quasiconformal reflection by the three-point/cross-ratio condition; §5 proves the boundary correspondence is quasisymmetric by extremal-distance estimates and invokes the Beurling–Ahlfors extension. The source reflection need not be an involution; this item constructs an involution separately from a quasiconformal circle image.

references.title: Frederick J. Gehring, Characterizations of quasidisks, Banach Center Publications 48 (1999), 11–41
references.locator: §II.B, printed pp. 17–18, Lemma 6 and Corollary 8: the two-point inequality and alternating four-point reversed triangle inequality are equivalent, with constants b=2M(M+1) and M=2b.

references.title: Mikhail Lyubich, Conformal Geometry and Dynamics of Quadratic Polynomials, vol. I (book draft, Stony Brook)
references.locator: Ch. 2 §15.3.1, Definition 15.9, printed pp. 209–210: bounded-turning definition of a quasicircle; used for the intrinsic condition and source terminology.

items.title: Conformally removable compact sets
items.statement: Write $\widehat{\mathbb C}=\mathbb C\cup\{\infty\}$ for the Riemann sphere with its standard holomorphic charts. A compact $K\subseteq\widehat{\mathbb C}$ is globally conformally removable (or CH-removable) if every homeomorphism $F:\widehat{\mathbb C}\to\widehat{\mathbb C}$ conformal on $\widehat{\mathbb C}\setminus K$ is a Möbius transformation. For a compact $K\subset\mathbb C$, Lyubich's neighborhood-local condition is that every homeomorphic embedding $h:U\to\mathbb C$ from every open neighborhood $U\supset K$, conformal on $U\setminus K$, is conformal on $U$. These are recorded separately; their equivalence is not asserted. Global conformal removability is monotone under compact subsets and invariant under Möbius changes of coordinates. No size condition is part of the definition.
items.strategy: The global definition is the CH-removable condition of Younsi Definition 1.1, while the neighborhood-local condition is Lyubich Definition 16.1. The source passages give different formulations; the scaffold's proposed extension of an arbitrary neighborhood embedding to a sphere homeomorphism does not establish their equivalence, so no equivalence or global-to-local implication is used here. Global subset monotonicity follows because a homeomorphism conformal off a compact subset $K'\subseteq K$ is also conformal off $K$. Möbius invariance follows by conjugating the test sphere homeomorphism; no Choice is used.

references.title: Mikhail Lyubich, Conformal Geometry and Dynamics of Quadratic Polynomials, vol. I, §16.1
references.locator: Ch. 2 §16.1, printed p. 215, Definition 16.1, the neighborhood-local formulation; read in full

references.title: Malik Younsi, On removable sets for holomorphic functions, §1
references.locator: §1, printed p. 221, Definition 1.1 and the monotonicity remark for CH-removable compact sets; read in full

items.title: Compact sets of finite length are removable for continuous analytic functions
items.axiom_use: Countable Choice is assumed for countable cover/center selections in the finite-length square-cover argument and for countable subadditivity of planar outer measure in the proof that planar squares have infinite one-dimensional Hausdorff measure. No full Choice use is claimed; the square-cover theorem's exact foundational strength remains under source review.
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice. If K is compact in the Riemann sphere with finite one-dimensional Hausdorff measure for the chordal metric, then every continuous f from the sphere to C that is holomorphic off K is constant. In particular this holds when H^1(K)=0.
items.strategy: Normalize by a Möbius map whose pole lies outside K, using the chordal bi-Lipschitz formula to preserve finite H^1, then work in a bounded plane square. The proof uses the finite-length square-cover input: arbitrarily small squares with disjoint interiors, K covered by their interiors, boundaries avoiding K, and uniformly bounded total side length. Cauchy's formula on the square with these holes gives the outer-contour representation; the modulus-of-continuity estimate makes the hole terms tend to zero, so f extends holomorphically across K and is constant by Liouville. Younsi §3.2 states this estimate in a proof sketch and directs the reader to Garnett, Chapter III, §II for the complete covering proof. That passage is unavailable in the current preview, so the square-cover prerequisite and its Choice strength remain escalated.

references.title: Malik Younsi, On removable sets for holomorphic functions, EMS Surveys in Mathematical Sciences 2 (2015), 219–254
references.locator: §3.2, Theorem 3.5 (Besicovitch) and Corollary 3.6, printed pp. 232–233; the finite-length proof is explicitly a sketch.

references.title: John B. Garnett, Analytic Capacity and Measure, Lecture Notes in Mathematics 297, Springer (1972)
references.locator: Chapter III, §II, the full square-covering proof cited by Younsi §3.2; unavailable in the current Springer preview, therefore still an open source obligation.

references.title: Lars Ahlfors and Arne Beurling, Conformal invariants and function-theoretic null-sets, Acta Mathematica 83 (1950), 101–129
references.locator: §6, Theorems 11 and 11′, printed pp. 121–122; zero-length linear and analytic-curve special cases only, not used to prove the general finite-length assertion.

items.title: Round circles and lines are conformally removable
items.axiom_use: Assume the Axiom of Choice to use the analytic ACL/Sobolev convention, the 1-quasiconformal/conformal theorem, and the smooth-line gluing theorem. Countable Choice is used inside those interfaces and follows from AC by [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]. The Möbius and subset arguments use no choice.
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Every compact subset $K$ of a straight line or a round circle in $\mathbb C$ is globally conformally removable ([[def-conformal-removable-compact-set]]). In particular, the round circle $\mathbb S^1$ and the generalized line $\mathbb R\cup\{\infty\}$ are conformally removable.
items.strategy: First prove the unit circle CH-removable: a homeomorphism conformal off the circle is chartwise analytically 1-quasiconformal there; the smooth-circle gluing theorem gives 1-quasiconformality on the sphere, and the one-quasiconformal/conformal theorem in local sphere charts makes the map biholomorphic and hence Möbius. Then use Möbius invariance to transfer the result to every round circle and every generalized line; subset monotonicity gives the compact-subset statement. The Younsi Jones–Smirnov shadow criterion is an alternative sufficient condition and is not used by this proof.

references.title: Mikhail Lyubich, Conformal Geometry and Dynamics of Quadratic Polynomials, vol. I (book draft, Stony Brook)
references.locator: Ch. 2 §16.1, printed p. 215: the source records in one sentence the classical removability of smooth Jordan curves but supplies no proof there. The present item supplies the argument using the smooth-circle gluing and 1-quasiconformal/conformal suppliers.

items.title: Compact sets of positive area are not conformally removable
items.axiom_use: Assume the Axiom of Choice for the measurable Riemann mapping theorem and the local one-quasiconformal/conformal interface. Countable Choice is used by the Beltrami, weak-solution, and Borel/Lebesgue interfaces; AC implies it by [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]].
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K\subseteq\widehat{\mathbb C}$ be compact and suppose its finite-chart part $E:=K\cap\mathbb C$ has positive planar Lebesgue area, $\lambda_2(E)>0$, using $\mathbb C\cong\mathbb R^2$ ([[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]], [[rem-complex-plane-euclidean-dictionary]]). Then there is a homeomorphism $F:\widehat{\mathbb C}\to\widehat{\mathbb C}$ conformal on $\widehat{\mathbb C}\setminus K$ that is not a Möbius transformation. Thus $K$ is not globally conformally removable ([[def-conformal-removable-compact-set]]), and every globally conformally removable compact set has zero area in the finite chart.
items.strategy: Take E=K intersected with the finite chart and prescribe the sphere Beltrami coefficient mu=1/2 on E and 0 off E. Compactness makes E Borel, Countable Choice gives Lebesgue measurability, and positive area makes ||mu||_infinity=1/2<1. Apply the measurable Riemann mapping theorem to obtain a sphere homeomorphism solving F_bar=mu F_z. The equation gives F_bar=0 on the complement of K, so local 1-quasiconformal/conformal equivalence makes F conformal there. A Mobius map has zero Beltrami coefficient, contradicting mu_F=mu=1/2 on E of positive area. The source's compressed assertion is expanded to show the chart, measurability, equation and non-Mobius steps explicitly.

references.title: Malik Younsi, On removable sets for holomorphic functions, EMS Surv. Math. Sci. 2 (2015) 219-254
references.locator: §4.2, Proposition 4.4 and the following remark, printed p. 235 / author-PDF p. 14: a Beltrami coefficient equal to 1/2 chi_E on a positive-area compact set gives a sphere homeomorphism conformal off E and not Möbius; the note states the same counterexample also rules out CH-removability.

references.title: Mikhail Lyubich, Conformal Geometry and Dynamics of Quadratic Polynomials, vol. I (book draft, Stony Brook)
references.locator: Ch. 2 §16.2, Proposition 16.4 and proof, printed p. 215: a removable set has zero area by solving a nontrivial Beltrami differential supported on it. The proof here spells out the coefficient, chart convention and non-Möbius contradiction.

items.title: Conformal removability is invariant under quasiconformal maps
items.axiom_use: Assume AC for the measurable Riemann mapping theorem, the analytic quasiconformal convention, composition/inversion, and the local 1-quasiconformal criterion. Countable Choice is used in the measurable coefficient and area interfaces and follows from AC by [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]].
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $h:\widehat{\mathbb C}\to\widehat{\mathbb C}$ be a quasiconformal homeomorphism. For every compact set $K\subseteq\widehat{\mathbb C}$, $K$ is globally conformally removable if and only if $h(K)$ is globally conformally removable ([[def-conformal-removable-compact-set]]).
items.strategy: Direct proof recorded in the item.

references.title: Malik Younsi, On removable sets for holomorphic functions, EMS Surv. Math. Sci. 2 (2015), 219–254
references.locator: §5.1, Proposition 5.3 and proof, printed pp. 241–242: quasiconformal invariance of CH-removability; the source assumes h(∞)=∞ and uses the measurable Riemann mapping theorem, null-set preservation, and Weyl's lemma. Section 4.1, Theorem 4.2, printed p. 234, supplies the Beltrami existence and uniqueness-up-to-conformal-map interface.

references.title: Mikhail Lyubich, Conformal Geometry and Dynamics of Quadratic Polynomials, vol. I (book draft, Stony Brook)
references.locator: Ch. 2 §§14.1–14.5, printed pp. 195–198: the sphere measurable Riemann mapping theorem, uniqueness, and the coefficient-straightening argument; read in full.

items.title: Zero-length compact sets and quasicircles are conformally removable
items.axiom_use: Assume AC for the round-circle and quasiconformal-invariance suppliers and the quasiconformal convention in the quasicircle definition. Countable Choice is used by the finite-Hausdorff-length continuous-analytic-removability supplier; it follows from AC by [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]. The normalization and quotient argument in part (a) uses no choice beyond that supplier's Countable Choice assumption.
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathcal H^1_\chi$ denote one-dimensional Hausdorff measure for the chordal metric on $\widehat{\mathbb C}$. Every compact set $K\subseteq\widehat{\mathbb C}$ with $\mathcal H^1_\chi(K)=0$ is globally conformally removable; the same proof shows this for every compact $K$ with $\mathcal H^1_\chi(K)<\infty$ ([[def-conformal-removable-compact-set]]).

Every quasicircle is globally conformally removable ([[def-quasicircle]]).

No converse and no Hausdorff-dimension threshold are asserted.
items.strategy: For (a), take a Mobius coordinate carrying a point outside K to infinity, preserving finite chordal H^1 by the explicit chordal formula. Normalize the target so F fixes infinity; the chart expression at infinity gives F(z)=az+b+O(1/z), a!=0. For finite z0 outside K, G(z)=(F(z)-F(z0))/(z-z0), with its derivative value at z0 and value a at infinity, is continuous on the sphere and holomorphic off K. Apply [[lem-zero-length-sets-are-removable-for-continuous-analytic-functions]] to make G constant and F affine, hence Mobius. For (b), write a quasicircle as h(S1); apply [[lem-round-circles-are-conformally-removable]] and transport removability through h using [[lem-conformal-removability-is-quasiconformally-invariant]].

references.title: Malik Younsi, On removable sets for holomorphic functions, EMS Surv. Math. Sci. 2 (2015) 219-254
references.locator: §3.2, Theorem 3.5, printed pp. 232-233: finite-H¹ sets are removable for continuous analytic functions, but the paper explicitly gives only a proof sketch and points to Garnett, Chapter III, §II for details; §5.1 Propositions 5.1 and 5.3, printed pp. 241-242, give A-removable implies CH-removable and quasiconformal invariance. The quotient proof cited by Proposition 5.1 is Proposition 4.3, printed pp. 235-236. The relevant passages were read; the finite-length covering proof remains an open source obligation.

references.title: Mikhail Lyubich, Conformal Geometry and Dynamics of Quadratic Polynomials, vol. I (book draft, Stony Brook)
references.locator: Ch. 2 §16.3, printed pp. 215-217, Lemma 16.3: quasicircles are removable; its stated route uses equivalence with quasiconformal removability and quasiconformal invariance. Section 16.1 uses a neighborhood-local formulation, while this item uses the library's explicitly global sphere formulation.

references.title: Christopher J. Bishop, Quasiconformal Mappings (Stony Brook Math 627 course notes, 164 pp.)
references.locator: Ch. 2 §7, Corollary 7.7, printed p. 76: in the section on quasiconformal removability, the quasicircle case is reduced to quasiconformal removability of the line by pre- and post-composition. This corroborates the QC-removability input only; the present proof uses the global CH-removability and QC-invariance suppliers.

items.title: The welding homeomorphism of a Jordan curve
items.axiom_use: The Axiom of Choice is inherited through Jordan–Brouwer separation and the Riemann-mapping/boundary-correspondence supplier. Countable Choice is included through that boundary lemma's extremal-length interfaces and follows from AC. For a fixed curve, choosing its two maps is finite choice; no further selection is used.
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathbb D=\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|<1\}$, $\mathbb T=\partial\mathbb D$, and $\mathbb D^*=\widehat{\mathbb C}\setminus\overline{\mathbb D}$. Identify $\mathbb S^1=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with $\mathbb T$ by $[t]\mapsto e^{2\pi it}$ ([[def-circle-as-real-line-mod-integers]], [[thm-real-line-mod-integers-is-homeomorphic-to-the-unit-circle]]). A Jordan curve is used in the sense of [[def-quasicircle]]; it has two complementary components with common boundary by [[thm-jordan-brouwer-separation]]. Fix an ordered pair of these components, denoted $\Omega_0,\Omega_1$.

The boundary-correspondence lemma ([[lem-riemann-maps-of-jordan-domains-extend-homeomorphically]]) supplies conformal equivalences $f:\mathbb D\to\Omega_0$ and $g:\mathbb D^*\to\Omega_1$ and unique homeomorphic extensions $\overline f:\overline{\mathbb D}\to\overline{\Omega_0}$ and $\overline g:\overline{\mathbb D^*}\to\overline{\Omega_1}$. Here maps between spherical domains are conformal in the holomorphic charts of the Riemann sphere ([[def-riemann-sphere-holomorphic-charts]]). Define the welding homeomorphism of $\Gamma$ for the chosen maps by
$$h_{\Gamma;f,g}:=(\overline f|_{\mathbb T})^{-1}\circ(\overline g|_{\mathbb T}):\mathbb T\to\mathbb T.$$

The map $h_{\Gamma;f,g}$ is orientation-preserving. An oriented conformal welding of an orientation-preserving homeomorphism $h:\mathbb T\to\mathbb T$ is a triple $(\Gamma,f,g)$ as above for which $h_{\Gamma;f,g}=h$. Equivalently, $\overline g|_{\mathbb T}=\overline f|_{\mathbb T}\circ h$. The convention $h=f^{-1}\circ g$ on the boundary is the inverse of the source convention $g^{-1}\circ f$.

The dependence on the parameter maps is a two-sided $\operatorname{Aut}(\mathbb D)$ action. Let $J(z)=1/z$, which maps $\mathbb D^*$ biholomorphically to $\mathbb D$. For $\alpha,\beta\in\operatorname{Aut}(\mathbb D)$, put $\beta^*:=J^{-1}\circ\beta\circ J\in\operatorname{Aut}(\mathbb D^*)$. Replacing $f$ by $f\circ\alpha$ and $g$ by $g\circ\beta^*$ changes the welding map to
$$h_{\Gamma;f\circ\alpha,g\circ\beta^*}=\alpha^{-1}|_{\mathbb T}\circ h_{\Gamma;f,g}\circ\beta^*|_{\mathbb T}.$$

Postcomposing both parameter maps with a Möbius transformation does not change the welding map: if $M$ is Möbius, the maps $M\circ f,M\circ g$ parameterize the correspondingly ordered components of $M(\Gamma)$ and $h_{M(\Gamma);M\circ f,M\circ g}=h_{\Gamma;f,g}$. No uniqueness of the welding curve is asserted here.
items.strategy: For a fixed ordered pair of complementary Jordan components, the boundary-correspondence lemma supplies disk maps and continuous one-to-one boundary extensions; composing the inverse of one boundary map with the other defines the welding homeomorphism. The disk/exterior boundary orientations reverse together, making this composition orientation-preserving. Precomposing the two component maps by disk automorphisms changes h by the derived two-sided action, while common postcomposition by a Möbius map cancels from f^{-1}g.

references.title: Christopher J. Bishop, Conformal welding and Koebe's theorem, Annals of Mathematics 166 (2007), 613–656
references.locator: §1, printed p. 613: disk/exterior parameterizations of the bounded/unbounded components and inverse convention g^{-1}∘f; read in full

references.title: Malik Younsi, On removable sets for holomorphic functions, EMS Surveys in Mathematical Sciences 2 (2015), 219–254
references.locator: §5.4, Definition 5.20 and the following paragraph on pre/post-composition and Möbius equivalence (author PDF p. 26); read in full

references.title: Mikhail Lyubich, Conformal Geometry and Dynamics of Quadratic Polynomials, vol. I (book draft, Stony Brook)
references.locator: Ch. 2 §15.4, printed pp. 212–214: component Riemann maps, transit map, orientation, two-sided automorphism and Möbius actions; read in full

items.title: Every quasisymmetric circle homeomorphism is a conformal welding
items.axiom_use: Assume AC. It is used by the Beurling–Ahlfors extension, the measurable Riemann mapping theorem, the analytic quasiconformal composition and coefficient interfaces, and smooth-circle gluing. Countable Choice is included in the measure interfaces for those suppliers; AC implies it by [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]].
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $h:\mathbb S^1\to\mathbb S^1$ be an orientation-preserving $L$-quasisymmetric homeomorphism ([[def-quasisymmetric-circle-homeomorphism]]).

(a) There is a conformal welding $(\Gamma_h,f,g)$ of $h$ in the convention of [[def-conformal-welding-of-a-jordan-curve]]. Its welding curve $\Gamma_h$ is a $K(L)$-quasicircle ([[def-quasicircle]]).

(b) In the construction below, the curve is independent of the chosen quasiconformal extension of $h$ to $\overline{\mathbb D}$: for any two such extensions, the corresponding measurable Riemann mapping solutions can be chosen so that their restrictions to $\mathbb S^1$ agree. The construction is invariant, up to the postcomposition ambiguity of the uniformizing map, under the two-sided $\operatorname{Aut}(\mathbb D)$ action on $h$. Thus the curve is determined up to postcomposition by a Möbius transformation.

This asserts existence and independence for the measurable-structure construction. It does not assert uniqueness of the welding curve among all possible weldings of $h$; that stronger statement requires an additional removability hypothesis.
items.strategy: Extend the boundary map to the disk, solve the Beltrami equation for its coefficient on the disk and the standard coefficient outside, then read off the two conformal maps from the uniformizing solution. The coefficient-side construction is written to match the inverse boundary convention in the library definition.

references.title: Mikhail Lyubich, Conformal Geometry and Dynamics of Quadratic Polynomials, vol. I (book draft, Stony Brook)
references.locator: Ch. 2 §15.4, Theorem 15.23 and proof, printed pp. 212–214, equations (15.3)–(15.7): Ahlfors–Beurling extension, measurable conformal structure, MRMT uniformization, independence from the extension, two-sided Möbius action, and recovery of the welding maps. The source uses the inverse boundary convention to this library; the item mirrors the coefficient construction to match [[def-conformal-welding-of-a-jordan-curve]]. The source’s broader uniqueness argument for arbitrary weldings is not used. Read in full.

items.title: Welding uniqueness for conformally removable curves
items.axiom_use: Assume AC for Jordan-domain uniformization/boundary correspondence and for the quasisymmetric-welding existence supplier used in part (b). Countable Choice used by those analytic and boundary interfaces follows from AC via [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]. The gluing and Möbius-removability argument in part (a) makes no further choice.
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $h:\mathbb S^1\to\mathbb S^1$ be an orientation-preserving homeomorphism, and let $(\Gamma,f,g)$ and $(\Gamma',f',g')$ be two conformal weldings of $h$ in the convention $h=f^{-1}\circ g$ of [[def-conformal-welding-of-a-jordan-curve]].

(a) If $\Gamma$ is globally conformally removable, then there is a Möbius transformation $A$ such that $f'=A\circ f$ and $g'=A\circ g$. In particular, $\Gamma'=A(\Gamma)$.

(b) If $h$ is quasisymmetric, then a welding with a quasicircle curve exists ([[thm-quasiconformal-welding-existence]]). Every other welding of $h$ has curve Möbius-equivalent to that quasicircle, so the welding curve is unique up to Möbius postcomposition.
items.strategy: Write each welding map using its homeomorphic boundary extensions and the library convention h=f^{-1}∘g. Equality of the two boundary maps implies f'∘f^{-1}=g'∘g^{-1} on Γ. Paste these conformal maps on the two closed complementary Jordan domains; the boundary identity makes the map and its inverse continuous, so it is a sphere homeomorphism conformal off Γ. If Γ is globally CH-removable this map is Möbius, giving f'=A∘f and g'=A∘g. For quasisymmetric h, the existence theorem supplies one quasicircle welding; the removability theorem makes its boundary removable, and the first part compares every other welding to it.

references.title: Malik Younsi, On removable sets for holomorphic functions, EMS Surveys in Mathematical Sciences 2 (2015), 219–254
references.locator: §5.4, Proposition 5.23 and Corollary 5.24, printed pp. 248–249: equality of welding classes gives a sphere homeomorphism conformal off the first boundary; when that boundary is CH-removable, the domains are Möbius-equivalent. The proof is read in full.

references.title: Mikhail Lyubich, Conformal Geometry and Dynamics of Quadratic Polynomials, vol. I (book draft, Stony Brook)
references.locator: Ch. 2 §15.4, printed pp. 213-214: the uniqueness step of Theorem 15.23, 'since quasicircles are removable, $\Phi$ is Möbius, so the structures are conformally equivalent'; read in full

references.title: Christopher J. Bishop, Conformal welding and Koebe's theorem, Ann. of Math. 166 (2007) 613-656
references.locator: §1, printed pp. 613–614: the introduction says the curve-to-welding map is not generally one-to-one and then describes flexible curves sharing a welding. This cautions against unconditional uniqueness and is not used as evidence for the removable-curve implication.

title: Quasisymmetry, Welding, and Conformal Removability: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: Power maps, endpoint distortion, and a non-Möbius quasisymmetric circle map
items.axiom_use: Assume AC only for the Beurling–Ahlfors extension suppliers in part (c). Their measure and ACL interfaces also use Countable Choice, which follows from AC by [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]. The power-map and circle-distortion calculations in parts (a) and (b) and the explicit quasisymmetric estimate in part (c) are choice free.
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. For $p>0$, define $h_p:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ by $h_p(x)=x^p$. For half-line quasisymmetry, use the adjacent-equal-interval inequality from [[def-quasisymmetric-circle-homeomorphism]], restricted to intervals contained in $[0,\infty)$.

(a) The map $h_p$ is an increasing homeomorphism of $[0,\infty)$ and is quasisymmetric with the sharp constant
$$L(p)=\max\{2^p-1,\,1/(2^p-1)\}.$$
At the endpoint, for $I=[0,t]$ and $J=[t,2t]$ with $t>0$,
$$\frac{|h_p(I)|}{|h_p(J)|}=\frac1{2^p-1}.$$
For $I_k=[kt,(k+1)t]$ and $J_k=[(k+1)t,(k+2)t]$,
$$\frac{|h_p(J_k)|}{|h_p(I_k)|}=\frac{(k+2)^p-(k+1)^p}{(k+1)^p-k^p}\longrightarrow1\qquad(k\to\infty).$$
For $p\ne1$, the sharp distortion larger than $1$ is attained at $k=0$ in the corresponding order; both ordered ratios tend to $1$ as $k\to\infty$. The map $h_p$ is affine exactly when $p=1$.

(b) The endpoint power completion $H_p:\mathbb S^1\to\mathbb S^1$ defined by the lift
$$\psi_p(\theta)=2\pi\left(\frac{\theta}{2\pi}\right)^p,\qquad 0\le\theta\le2\pi,$$
is a homeomorphism fixing $1$. If $p\ne1$, it is not quasisymmetric: adjacent arcs of equal length on opposite sides of $1$ have image-length ratio tending to $0$ or $+\infty$ as their length tends to zero.

(c) For $0<\delta<1$, the circle map
$$h_\delta(e^{i\theta})=e^{i(\theta+\delta\sin\theta)}$$
is an orientation-preserving quasisymmetric homeomorphism with constant at most $(1+\delta)/(1-\delta)$, and it is not the restriction of any Möbius transformation. It extends to a quasiconformal homeomorphism of the disc. Explicitly, if $f_\delta(t)=t+\delta\sin t$ and $G_\delta$ is its reflected Ahlfors–Beurling line extension, then the circle extension is
$$\widetilde h_\delta(e^{iz})=e^{iG_\delta(z)}.$$
items.strategy: For (a), homogeneity reduces adjacent intervals to the ratio $R_p(s)=((s+1)^p-s^p)/((s+2)^p-(s+1)^p)$; convexity/concavity and chord bounds show the sharp two-order constant is $\max\{2^p-1,1/(2^p-1)\}$. The mean value theorem gives the stated limit of the reverse ratios and the second derivative settles affinity. For (b), compare the equal arcs on either side of the fixed point; their image lengths are asymptotic to a constant times $t^p$ and to $pt$. For (c), the lift $t+\delta\sin t$ has derivative in $[1-\delta,1+\delta]$, and its angular derivatives at $0$ and $\pi$ rule out a disk automorphism. Descend the explicit reflected Ahlfors–Beurling extension through $e^{iz}$; the Beurling–Ahlfors circle supplier gives its quasiconformal extension over $0$ and $\infty$.

references.title: Mikhail Lyubich, Conformal Geometry and Dynamics of Quadratic Polynomials, vol. I (book draft, Stony Brook)
references.locator: Ch. 2 §15.1.1, printed p. 207, Exercise 15.1(i)-(ii): the exercise states that positive power maps on [0,1] are quasisymmetric and that matching a power map to the identity across the endpoint can destroy quasisymmetry, but supplies no proof. The present item gives the adjacent-interval ratios and the circle endpoint calculation in full.

items.title: The Koch snowflake is a non-rectifiable quasicircle
items.axiom_use: Assume AC for the quasicircle-characterisation and conformal-removability suppliers. Countable Choice, derived from AC, is used for the Lebesgue measure and outer-measure interfaces in the Hausdorff-measure estimate.
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Normalize an equilateral triangle to have side length $1$, and construct the classical Koch snowflake $S$ by replacing the middle third of every boundary segment by the two sides of the outward equilateral bump at each stage. Equivalently, $S$ is the Hausdorff limit of the snowflake polygons $P_n$. Then:

(a) $S$ is a Jordan curve with bounded-turning constant $M=12$, hence is a quasicircle.

(b) $P_n$ has perimeter $3(4/3)^n$, which tends to infinity. Thus $S$ is not rectifiable, its chord-arc (Lavrentiev) condition fails (a chord-arc Jordan curve is rectifiable and has shorter-subarc length bounded by a constant times chord length), and quasicircles need not be rectifiable.

(c) With $s=\log 4/\log 3$, one has $0<\mathcal H^s(S)<\infty$, $\dim_H S=s$, and $\mathcal H^1(S)=+\infty$.

(d) $S$ is conformally removable.
items.strategy: Use the four-similarity rhombus cells and base-four parametrisation of each Koch side. The classical all-outward parametrisation is injective on the circle, and the complete case split in the cited source proves bounded turning with constant 12, including adjacent cells at a fjord and cells on different sides. Retained polygon vertices give perimeter $3(4/3)^n$ and nonrectifiability. The cell cover gives finite $\mathcal H^s$; for the lower bound, pack one inscribed square into each level-$n$ rhombus, compare areas to bound the number of cells meeting a set, and pull covers back to the base-four intervals in $[0,1]$. Positive finite critical measure gives the dimension and infinite $\mathcal H^1$. The quasicircle and removability conclusions use the two cited authored suppliers.

references.title: Mikhail Lyubich, Conformal Geometry and Dynamics of Quadratic Polynomials, vol. I (book draft, Stony Brook)
references.locator: Ch. 1 §1.4.1, printed pp. 22–23: the classical Koch snowflake construction and its self-similar sides; read in full

references.title: S. van Golden, S. Kombrink, and T. Samuel, On the geometry of generalised Koch snowflakes
references.locator: §2, Lemma 2.1 and the Hausdorff-dimension proof, printed pp. 4–7: the four ratio-1/3 rhombus cells, disjoint interiors, and the finite-positive critical Hausdorff measure argument; §3, Lemma 3.1, Proposition 3.2 and Theorem 3.3, printed pp. 6–9: the classical snowflake parametrisation, Jordan property, complete cell-based bounded-turning proof, and constant 12. The full relevant arguments were read.

references.title: M. Ghomi, Curves and Surfaces, Lecture Notes 1
references.locator: Exercise 9: the Koch-side polygonal construction and the hint that its approximants have lengths tending to infinity. The exercise is not used as a proof; the retained-vertex polygonal-sum argument is given in Proof 1.2.

items.title: The identity welding of the round circle
items.axiom_use: Assume AC for the Jordan-boundary and conformal-removability/uniqueness interfaces. The identity welding and the disk-automorphism calculations use no further choice.
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathbb D=\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|<1\}$ and $\mathbb T=\partial\mathbb D$, with $\mathbb D^*=\widehat{\mathbb C}\setminus\overline{\mathbb D}$. Set $\Gamma=\mathbb T$, $\Omega_0=\mathbb D$, $\Omega_1=\mathbb D^*$, and take $f=\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb D}$ and $g=\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb D^*}$. In the library convention $h=f^{-1}\circ g|_{\mathbb T}$, this gives $h=\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb T}$, so the identity circle homeomorphism is welded by the round circle.

More generally, for $A,B\in\operatorname{Aut}(\mathbb D)$ let $\widetilde A,\widetilde B$ be their standard Möbius extensions to the sphere, and set $f=A:\mathbb D\to\mathbb D$ and $g=\widetilde B|_{\mathbb D^*}:\mathbb D^*\to\mathbb D^*$. Then the welding is the Möbius circle homeomorphism $h=\widetilde A^{-1}\circ\widetilde B|_{\mathbb T}$, and $h=\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb T}$ if and only if $A=B$.

Every welding of $\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb T}$ has a generalized round circle as its welding curve: it is the image of $\mathbb T$ under a Möbius transformation, hence is either a Euclidean circle or a straight line together with $\infty$.
items.strategy: Compute the boundary compositions in the library convention $h=f^{-1}\circ g$. The disk-automorphism theorem gives sphere Möbius extensions preserving both complementary sides, so their boundary composition is the stated Möbius circle map; fixing every boundary point forces the two maps to agree. For an arbitrary welding of the identity, apply conditional welding uniqueness with the removable round circle as the first curve. The resulting Möbius image of $\mathbb T$ is a generalized circle.

references.title: Christopher J. Bishop, Conformal welding and Koebe's theorem, Ann. of Math. 166 (2007) 613-656
references.locator: §1, printed pp. 613–614: the source convention h=g^{-1}∘f, the statement that a welding need not determine its curve uniquely, and the flexible-curve example. These are convention/context only; the present example verifies its explicit identity pair directly.

references.title: Malik Younsi, On removable sets for holomorphic functions, EMS Surv. Math. Sci. 2 (2015) 219-254
references.locator: §5.4, Definition 5.22 and the following paragraph on pre/post-composition by disk automorphisms and Möbius equivalence, printed pp. 247–248; Corollary 5.24 and its proof, printed pp. 248–249: a CH-removable welding boundary determines its Jordan domain up to Möbius transformation. Read in full.

references.title: Mikhail Lyubich, Conformal Geometry and Dynamics of Quadratic Polynomials, vol. I (book draft, Stony Brook)
references.locator: Ch. 2 §15.4, printed pp. 212–213: the connected-sum definition of welding, the two-sided disk-automorphism action, and Theorem 15.23's Möbius uniqueness for quasiconformal welding. Read in full; the library's boundary convention is stated separately.

items.title: The Möbius ambiguity in conformal welding
items.axiom_use: Assume AC for the Jordan-boundary and conformal-removability/uniqueness interfaces. The explicit Möbius weldings and algebraic normalizations use no further choice.
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathbb D$ be the unit disk, $\mathbb T=\partial\mathbb D$, and $\mathbb D^*=\widehat{\mathbb C}\setminus\overline{\mathbb D}$. Let $h:\mathbb T\to\mathbb T$ be an orientation-preserving Möbius circle homeomorphism, and write $H$ for its Möbius extension to the sphere. Then $H$ preserves $\mathbb D$ and $\mathbb D^*$. With $f=\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb D}$ and $g=H|_{\mathbb D^*}$, the round circle is a welding curve for $h$. For example, $h(\zeta)=(\zeta-a)/(1-\overline a\zeta)$ for $a\in\mathbb D$ is the boundary map of a disk automorphism and is welded by the round circle.

For a fixed $h$, simultaneous postcomposition of both parameter maps by a Möbius transformation leaves the welding map unchanged and carries the welding curve to its Möbius image. In particular, any two weldings of $h$ with the round circle as curve differ by a common Möbius postcomposition.

Every welding curve for $h$ is a Möbius image of $\mathbb T$. Fixing the images of three distinct boundary points removes the common Möbius ambiguity and gives a unique normalized welding.
items.strategy: A Möbius extension of an orientation-preserving circle map must preserve the disk, since interchanging disk and exterior reverses the induced boundary orientation. Thus the identity map inside and the given extension outside realize the welding. Removability of the round circle and conditional welding uniqueness give the postcomposition action and show every other curve is a Möbius image; three-point normalization removes that action.

references.locator: §1, printed pp. 613–614: the normalization qualifications in the definition and the fact that the curve-to-welding map is not generally one-to-one. Read in full.

items.title: Not every compact set is conformally removable
items.axiom_use: Assume AC for the round-circle and positive-area removability suppliers. Countable Choice is used by the Lebesgue product and measure interfaces for the planar fat-Cantor example; it follows from AC by [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]. The explicit radial counterexample is choice free.
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). The closed unit disk $\overline{\mathbb D}:=\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|\le1\}$ is a compact set that is not globally conformally removable ([[def-conformal-removable-compact-set]]). A witness is the sphere map
$$F(z)=\begin{cases}z(1+|z|)/2,&|z|\le1,\\z,&|z|\ge1,\end{cases}\qquad F(\infty)=\infty.$$
It fixes $\mathbb S^1:=\{z:|z|=1\}$ pointwise and is conformal on $\widehat{\mathbb C}\setminus\overline{\mathbb D}$, while it is not Möbius. The boundary $\mathbb S^1$ is conformally removable ([[lem-round-circles-are-conformally-removable]]).

More generally, every compact sphere set with positive planar area in the finite chart is not conformally removable ([[lem-positive-area-compact-sets-are-not-conformally-removable]]). Such examples need not have interior: the product of two positive-length Smith–Volterra–Cantor sets is a compact positive-area set with empty interior.

There are also nonremovable Jordan curves of zero area: Bishop's flexible-curve theorem yields one with zero two-dimensional Hausdorff measure and hence zero planar area. This comparison is not needed for the explicit disk witness.
items.strategy: Construct the disk witness by a strictly increasing radial change of variables and verify its inverse, boundary values, and conformality off the disk. Use the positive-area obstruction for general compact sets and for a compact empty-interior product of fat Cantor sets.

references.title: Mikhail Lyubich, Conformal Geometry and Dynamics of Quadratic Polynomials, vol. I (book draft, Stony Brook)
references.locator: Ch. 2 §16.1–16.2, printed p. 215: Definition 16.1, the classical smooth-Jordan-curve removability observation, and Proposition 16.4 on area. Lyubich’s Definition 16.1 is neighborhood-local; this item uses the separately stated global CH definition and proves its disk witness directly. Read in full.

references.title: Malik Younsi, On removable sets for holomorphic functions, EMS Surveys in Mathematical Sciences 2 (2015), 219–254
references.locator: §4.2, Proposition 4.4 and Remark 4.5, printed p. 235: positive-area compact sets are not CH-removable by MRMT; §5.2, Theorem 5.17, printed pp. 244–245: Bishop’s nonremovable zero-area Jordan-curve theorem and the survey proof sketch. The proof details are checked against Bishop’s original article below. Read in full.

references.title: Christopher J. Bishop, Some homeomorphisms of the sphere conformal off a curve, Annales Academiæ Scientiarum Fennicæ Mathematica 19 (1994), 323–338
references.locator: Theorem 2, printed p. 324, and its construction in §§3–4, printed pp. 330–334: for each gauge h(t)=o(t), the construction yields a non-Möbius sphere homeomorphism conformal off a Jordan curve Γ with Λ_h(Γ)=0. Taking h(t)=t² gives a zero-area nonremovable Jordan curve. The paper’s auxiliary conformal-filling step is described briefly as an easy modification; this result is a nonessential comparison and is not used in the disk proof. Read in full.

items.title: A single point is conformally removable
items.statement: Every finite subset P of the Riemann sphere is globally conformally removable: each sphere homeomorphism conformal off P is Möbius. This includes every singleton. Moreover, finite P has zero one-dimensional Hausdorff measure for the chordal metric.
items.strategy: For each p in the finite exceptional set, use a Möbius domain chart taking p to 0 and a Möbius target chart taking F(p) to 0. The transformed map is sphere-continuous with a bounded finite coordinate on a punctured disk, so the removable-singularity characterization fills the point. This shows F holomorphic at every exceptional point; injectivity gives holomorphic local inverses, and every biholomorphic sphere self-map is Möbius. A finite family of small chordal balls directly shows H^1(P)=0. The scaffold route omitted target normalization and incorrectly inferred boundedness when F(p)=infinity; the proof now handles both finite and infinite values explicitly. No Choice is used.

references.title: Mikhail Lyubich, Conformal Geometry and Dynamics of Quadratic Polynomials, vol. I
references.locator: Ch. 2 §16.1, printed p. 215: Definition 16.1 and the statement that isolated points are classically conformally removable; contextual, while the authored proof uses the removable-singularity supplier.

references.title: Malik Younsi, On removable sets for holomorphic functions, EMS Surveys in Mathematical Sciences 2 (2015), 219–254
references.locator: §2.1, printed p. 222: one point and finite sets are removable for bounded holomorphic functions by Riemann’s theorem; this related scalar-valued class is not the CH proof used here.
